name: Calculating the Average of the Values in the List
description: Construct a program that has a function that receives a list and calculates the average of the values in that list. The program should handle lists with arbitrary number of values (including an empty list).
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def calculate_list_average(lst):
    #Step 1.1: Assign initial value to the variable which we need for this program
    total = 0
    #Step 1.2: Iterate through the list values and add each value to the running total
    for x in lst:
        total += x
    #Step 1.3: Calculate and print the average of the list values
    if len(lst) == 0 :
        print("The list has no values.")
    else :
        average = total / len(lst)
        print("Average is:", average)
#Step 2: Call the function
values = [6, 15, 9, 12, 1, 8]
calculate_list_average(values)

commentList: You compute the average here by dividing the running sum (total) by the number of items (len(lst)); the result is stored in the variable average so you can use or display it later.

Watch out for non-numeric list elements: if lst contains strings or other non-numbers, you or Python will get an error earlier or an incorrect result. Make sure the list contains numeric types before this division.

As a best practice, consider returning average from the function instead of printing it here (return average). That makes your function more reusable and easier for you to test. You can also simplify the computation with average = sum(lst) / len(lst) if you prefer concise code.

distractors.description: Step-by-step: you might pick this because you know functions often return values and you think returning is more flexible. This line is syntactically correct and will cause the function to hand the numeric average back to its caller. However, in the program as written the caller does not capture or print that returned value; the call simply invokes the function and the returned value is ignored. As a result, nothing will be shown on the screen even though the calculation succeeded. You may be misled into thinking that returning equals printing; the real difference is that returning passes data back to the caller while printing sends it to standard output. Using this line changes the program's behavior (no visible output) rather than producing the message you likely expect.

You might choose this because you think explicitly restating a condition makes the logic clearer or that an elif is required after an if. Step-by-step: the first if already checks whether the list is empty. If that test is True, that branch runs and the new elif will never be reached. If the first test is False (the list is non-empty), then this elif condition is also False, so its block does not run either. As a result, when the list has values, neither branch runs to compute the average and your function will skip producing the average. This is wrong because you have duplicated the same check instead of providing a branch that handles the opposite case. The key issue is misunderstanding how chained if/elif/else works: elif only runs when the prior conditions were False, so repeating the same condition defeats the purpose.

You might pick this because you believe the average should be an integer, or you confuse the floor-division operator with normal division. Step-by-step: this line uses floor (integer) division, so any fractional part of the true average is discarded rather than preserved. As a result, for lists whose sum is not evenly divisible by the count, you'll get a smaller, rounded-down value instead of the real average; the program will still run but produce an incorrect numeric result. Compared with the intended calculation, this line mishandles fractional results by truncating them; that key behavior (preserving the fraction) is missing here, which makes this choice incorrect.
